theme: The stolen blessing; Jacob’s ladder, election and promise
readingInstruction: Read Genesis 27:1-28:22. These chapters tell the story of Jacob stealing Esau’s blessing, his flight from his brother’s wrath, and his vision of the ladder at Bethel. Notice the messiness of God’s election, Jacob is a deceiver, and yet God claims him as the bearer of the covenant.
settingTheScene: Isaac is old and nearly blind. He plans to bless Esau, his favorite son, before he dies. But Rebekah overhears and concocts a scheme: Jacob will pretend to be Esau and steal the blessing. The deception works. When Esau discovers it, he plans to kill Jacob, so Jacob flees to Rebekah’s family in the east. On the way, he has a dream, the famous vision of the ladder reaching to heaven, with angels ascending and descending, and the LORD himself standing above. This is one of the most theologically rich dreams in the Old Testament.
observation: Isaac wants to bless Esau, his favorite, despite God’s word that the older would serve the younger.
Rebekah’s deception is elaborate, goat skins on Jacob’s hands, Esau’s clothes on his body, savory food disguised as game.
Isaac is suspicious but ultimately deceived. He blesses Jacob, thinking he is Esau.
Esau’s grief is real and intense: “Bless me, even me also, O my father!” He weeps bitterly.
Isaac’s second blessing on Esau is much weaker, Esau will live by the sword and serve his brother.
Esau plans to kill Jacob “as soon as Father is dead.” Murderous intent toward a brother, echoes of Cain.
Jacob flees to Haran, sent by his parents on the pretext of finding a wife.
On the way, alone in the wilderness, Jacob has the dream of the ladder.
The angels ascend and descend on the ladder. The LORD stands above and renews the covenant promise.
Jacob’s response: “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it.” Awe meets reality.
He names the place Bethel (“house of God”) and vows that if God brings him back safely, the LORD will be his God.
interpretation:
Genesis 27 and 28 are a study in the messiness of God’s election. Jacob is not a hero. He is a deceiver, manipulating his blind father, profiting from his mother’s scheme, stealing what God had already chosen to give him. And yet God meets him on the run and renews the covenant. This is the doctrine of grace in narrative form. God’s choice does not wait for moral worthiness. It operates on the basis of his own purposes.

The deception in Genesis 27 is excruciating to read. Rebekah, who knew from the womb that Jacob would be the chosen one, does not trust God to bring it about. So she takes matters into her own hands. She prepares the deception. She gives Jacob detailed instructions. She even takes the blame herself: “Let your curse be on me, my son.” Jacob, more cautious than committed, hesitates only because he might get caught, not because the deception is wrong. The scheme works. Isaac is fooled. Jacob receives the blessing meant for Esau.

The aftermath is devastating. Esau returns with the game he had hunted. Isaac trembles when he realizes what has happened. Esau cries out, one of the most painful cries in Scripture: “Bless me, even me also, O my father!” Hebrews 12 records what happened next: “He found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears.” The blessing once given could not be undone. Isaac speaks a secondary, lesser blessing over Esau, but the primary blessing is gone.

And then comes the consequence. Esau plans to kill Jacob. Rebekah, learning of this, sends Jacob away. The mother who manipulated to get her son the blessing now loses him, perhaps forever, the text suggests she never sees him again. The patriarchal family is fractured by deceit. Jacob flees with nothing but his staff. His scheming has cost him home, mother, father, and brother.

But God meets him on the road. In the wilderness, alone, with a stone for a pillow, Jacob has the dream. A ladder is set up between earth and heaven. The angels of God are ascending and descending on it. And the LORD stands above the ladder and speaks: “I am the LORD, the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac… and in you and your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.”

The covenant has just been renewed, to Jacob the deceiver, on the run, with nothing to commend him. This is grace. The same God who chose Jacob in the womb is choosing Jacob still. The promises made to Abraham, renewed to Isaac, are now passed to Jacob. The man does not deserve them. God gives them anyway. That is the definition of grace.

The image of the ladder is rich. It is the meeting place of heaven and earth. Angels move between the two realms. The God who seemed distant when Jacob fled is right above him. Centuries later, Jesus will tell Nathanael, “You will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man” (John 1:51). Jesus is the true ladder. He is the meeting place of heaven and earth. The dream Jacob saw was a preview of the incarnation. Jesus is the ladder that brings heaven down to those who are running from their own messes.

Jacob’s response is awe. “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it… This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.” He renames the place Bethel, “house of God.” And he makes a vow: “If God will be with me and will keep me… then the LORD shall be my God.” It is a tentative response, half faith, half bargaining. Jacob is not yet the man he will become. But God has met him, and the journey toward transformation has begun.
connection: The covenant has now been renewed to all three patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Each time, God renews it freely, despite the failures of the recipients. Jacob’s ladder will become one of the great Christological images of the Old Testament: Jesus is the true ladder, the meeting place of heaven and earth, the one in whom the promises to Abraham finally find their fulfillment.
application: If God only worked through moral heroes, none of us would qualify. Jacob was a manipulator. Rebekah was a schemer. Isaac was favoring the wrong son. Esau was profane. And in the middle of this dysfunctional family, God’s grace ran on, choosing, renewing, blessing. Today, take comfort from the fact that the God of Jacob is the God of imperfect people. He is not waiting for you to clean up your act before he meets you on the road. He is the God who shows up at Bethel, wherever you are, however you got there, with whatever stones you have for pillows. Look up. The ladder is open. Christ is the meeting place. And the same covenant promises are spoken over you.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he meets imperfect people on the run, and tell him where you have been running.
Thank Christ as the true ladder between heaven and earth.
Ask him to speak to you in your own wilderness.
